source.title: High-dimensional analysis of double descent for linear regression with random projections

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes test excess risk for minimum-norm linear regression with random projections, using a high-dimensional random-matrix method rather than testing deep networks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports asymptotic risk results and random-projection experiments as the number of projections m varies. Figure 3 is described as comparing asymptotic equivalents with finite-sample estimates; its text does not specify a double-descent outcome, so it is not separately cataloged. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The paper derives asymptotic bias and variance for min-norm least squares with a varying number m of random projections on a fixed problem. It shows risk rising to a peak at m=n and falling again for m>n, checked against simulations (Figs 1, 4, 5). This is a theoretical and simulation test of the general double-descent curve in a non-deep model class.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. The author proves a double descent for a fixed problem as m varies. The variance rises, explodes at m=n, then falls. The bias may be U-shaped for m<n, blows up at m=n, and then decreases. Above the threshold both terms decrease, so larger m is always better. In the isotropic case the under-parameterized risk only increases.
record.recipe_differences: High-dimensional random-matrix analysis and experiments for linear regression with random projections; not a reproduction of the deep-network or other original-source methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The under-parameterized bias shape depends on the covariance setting: the non-isotropic example has a U-shaped bias curve, while the isotropic example does not. The paper also distinguishes the m<n and m>n regimes.
record.peer_reviewed: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science
record.problems: The experimental illustrations cover specific covariance and signal settings, and plotted results are mostly not accompanied by exact numerical values in the text. The asymptotic theory relies on stated high-dimensional assumptions; the paper does not test deep networks, training epochs, or sample-size sweeps.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3 compares finite-sample estimates with asymptotic equivalents for bias and variance, but its text describes convergence rather than a specific double-descent result; it was not separately extracted.

untested.parts: Sweeps over training-sample count at fixed model size.
Model classes other than linear regression with random projections.
A single complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epochs and samples.
Label-noise sweeps, multiple peaks, and explicit tests of tuned regularization removing the peak in the projection model.
Re-plotting risk against effective parameters to test whether the curve becomes U-shaped. Degrees of freedom are used only as analytic quantities.

missing.what: The squared-bias term (σ=0) explodes at m=n via the 1/(1−m/n) factor. This shows a peak without label noise.
missing.locator: Section 1 (Introduction, last bullet); Section 6, Proposition 4 and the observations after it

missing.what: Remark that at the optimal ridge parameter the exploding term 1/(1−df2/n) usually disappears. This bears on whether tuned regularization removes the peak.
missing.locator: Section 4.2, after the proof of Proposition 3

record.verdict_notes: Tranche could arguably be T3 (new setting). The study is asymptotic theory with Matlab simulations that closely match the theory. Plotted values are not given numerically. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Changing training-sample count near the interpolation threshold.
The paper tests random-projection linear regression only; it does not compare model classes or establish that the behavior holds across model classes generally.
No comparison of one effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epoch, and sample axes.
No systematic sweep of label noise or optimally tuned regularization, and no test for multiple peaks.
The paper uses degrees of freedom in its analysis but does not test whether counting effective parameters turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.check: In the isotropic case only the under-parameterized U-shape is missing. The text says overall performance 'always goes up' for m<n, then blows up at m=n and decreases for m>n. So the peak and second descent are present and only the classical first descent is absent. 'Absent' overstates this; partial fits better. The locator should also cite the Section 6 observations after Prop. 4.

relationships.condition: Random-projection min-norm linear regression, non-isotropic covariance (eigenvalues ∝1/k), n=200, d=400
relationships.reason: The variance explodes at m=n and decreases for m>n (R1, R4). Bias and variance both decrease for m>n (R2). Bias is U-shaped for m<n (R5). Fig. 1 shows the full double-descent curve (R3).
relationships.display_finding: Variance diverged at m=n and declined alongside bias for m>n, while bias was U-shaped for m<n and total risk showed double descent.
